channel.title: Medical Xpress - latest medical and health news stories
channel.description: Medical Xpress internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: Workplace ergonomics may do little to ease arm, neck or shoulder pain
item.description: An updated Cochrane review has found that ergonomic interventions show no meaningful benefit for pain, function, recovery or sick leave in workers with work-related complaints of the arm, neck or shoulder (CANS), compared with no treatment.

item.title: Novel alpha radiopharmaceutical therapy shows promise in early-phase prostate cancer trial
item.description: A new alpha-emitting radiopharmaceutical therapy (RPT) for advanced prostate cancer was well tolerated, with no dose-limiting toxicities observed, and showed encouraging signs of antitumor activity, according to a trial published in The Journal of Nuclear Medicine's Late-Breaking Fast Track.

item.title: Needle-free Strep A vaccine triggers local and bodywide immune responses in mice
item.description: New research by the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) in partnership with the GSK Vaccines Institute for Global Health has moved a vaccine against the highly contagious group A streptococcus bacterium (Strep A) a step closer to reality.

item.title: Wearable EEG patch records stable brain signals over 24 hours, including sleep
item.description: Reliably recording brain activity over many hours has so far been fraught with technical and practical challenges. While traditional electroencephalography (EEG) systems provide meaningful data, they are often uncomfortable and typically limited to controlled testing environments. Is it even possible to record EEG signals with good signal quality in everyday situations?

item.title: How socioeconomic factors affect outcomes in this deadly cancer
item.description: Black women diagnosed with hormone receptor–positive (HR+) breast cancer experience significantly worse outcomes than white women.

item.title: Autistic women experience more severe menopausal symptoms, study confirms
item.description: A new study by researchers at Bournemouth University has shown that autistic people consistently experience more severe menopausal symptoms than non-autistic people, leading to poorer well-being and quality of life.

item.title: Q&A: Could a new melanoma vaccine change cancer treatment?
item.description: A personalized melanoma vaccine, called intismeran, could mark a major advance in cancer treatment. Last week, pharmaceutical companies Merck and Moderna announced clinical trial results showing the vaccine, combined with immunotherapy, reduced the risk of cancer returning or death by 42% compared with immunotherapy alone.

item.title: ADHD medication amplifies brain response to grammatically ambiguous sentences, study finds
item.description: In a neuroimaging study published in PNAS, a team of researchers led by the Max Planck Institute for Psycholinguistics in Nijmegen recorded the brain activity of healthy adults during sentence comprehension after raising catecholamine levels with stimulant medication (methylphenidate). Higher catecholamine levels led to stronger recruitment of cognitive resources during processing of grammatically ambiguous sentences, showing how neurochemical systems may shape language processing.

item.title: Night shifts during pregnancy linked to heightened risk of young child's neurodevelopmental abnormalities
item.description: Working night shifts during pregnancy is linked to a heightened risk of neurodevelopmental abnormalities detected by screening in the child by the age of 4, finds research published online in Occupational & Environmental Medicine.

item.title: Low-carb diet high in saturated fat shows mixed effects on cholesterol in two-year trial
item.description: New analyses from the Norwegian randomized controlled trial CARBFUNC show that more than doubling saturated fat intake over a two-year period can promote favorable changes in several cardiovascular risk markers, without increasing apoB, the main suspected risk factor. ApoB is a protein found in the particles that transport cholesterol in the blood and can be used to assess the risk of cardiovascular disease.

item.title: Neural network spots previously missed epilepsy signs on brain MRIs
item.description: Researchers from the joint Biomedically-Informed AI Laboratory of Skoltech (a VEB.RF Group institution) and the University of Sharjah and their colleagues have improved the performance of computer vision algorithms that look for signs of epilepsy and multiple sclerosis on brain MRI scans. Rather than merely analyzing an image as a set of pixels, the neural network now also attends to medical features known to physicians. This is complemented by the machine's capability to spot subtle details that elude the human eye. In the future, such solutions will help doctors diagnose diseases and select treatment strategies.

item.title: National study finds decline in drug use–associated heart infections but growing share involves stimulants
item.description: A new national study found that hospitalizations for serious heart infections associated with drug use are declining after years of increases, driven largely by a decrease in opioid-associated cases.

item.title: Targeting fat-cell enzyme offers potential strategy to reduce obesity and cancer risk
item.description: Obesity touches countless lives across the country and can lead to many other health complications. From August 2021 to 2023, the prevalence of obesity in adults in the U.S. was more than 40%. Research published in Science Advances, led by scientists at VCU Massey Comprehensive Cancer Center, found that targeting fat cells specifically with inhibitors of the enzyme sphingosine kinase 2 could be a new strategy to combat obesity and lower the risk of its comorbidities like cancer.

item.title: 3D-printed implant prototype combines brain activity recording with targeted cooling
item.description: Researchers affiliated with the Leibniz Institute of Polymer Research Dresden (IPF) and the Else Kröner Fresenius Center (EKFZ) for Digital Health at TU Dresden have developed a 3D-printed implant prototype that combines the recording of brain activity with targeted cooling. The technology could pave the way for alternative approaches to treating drug-resistant focal epilepsy. The research is published in the journal Advanced Science.

item.title: Guideline on shorter-course radiation therapy for localized prostate cancer updated
item.description: An updated clinical guideline from the American Society for Radiation Oncology (ASTRO) provides evidence-based recommendations on the use of hypofractionated radiation therapy for patients with localized prostate cancer. The guideline replaces ASTRO's 2018 recommendations and reflects a matured evidence base showing that shorter-course radiation therapy can maintain cancer control while reducing overall treatment burden for patients receiving definitive external beam radiation therapy (EBRT). The guideline was published in Practical Radiation Oncology.

item.title: How our blood vessels age from within
item.description: With every heartbeat, blood is pumped through a vast network of vessels throughout our body, delivering vital oxygen, nutrients and other essential substances to even its most remote corners. But these vessels are far more than passive tubes: Their inner walls are covered by a thin layer of specialized cells called endothelial cells, which regulate blood flow, control what passes into surrounding tissues and help coordinate responses to injury.

item.title: More than half of children under 5 exposed to hep B exposed via household contact
item.description: More than half of children younger than 5 years exposed to hepatitis B virus (HBV) are exposed by someone in their household other than their birth mother, according to a study presented at the annual meeting of the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDWeek), held from Oct. 21 to 24 in Washington, D.C.

item.title: Rising rates of colorectal cancer found in nearly all age groups
item.description: Colorectal cancer rates are rising across younger and older age groups, according to a study published in NEJM Evidence.

item.title: A doctor's take on new menopause guidelines
item.description: Many women I see in my practice have questions about menopause and hormone therapy. The newest guidelines from the American College of Obstetricians & Gynecologists (ACOG) bring some welcome clarity.

item.title: IDSA: Cabotegravir + rilpivirine long-acting antiretroviral therapy beneficial in HIV
item.description: Cabotegravir + rilpivirine (CAB+RPV) long-acting (LA) antiretroviral therapy (ART) consistently maintains virologic suppression among virologically suppressed adults with HIV, according to a study presented at the annual meeting of the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDWeek), held from Oct. 21 to 24 in Washington, D.C.

item.title: Deep brain stimulation improves new neuron maturation for memory
item.description: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) has traditionally been used to treat movement disorders and more recently some mental health disorders such as certain forms of depression, but research has suggested it can affect learning and memory as well.

item.title: Summer's produce outbreaks expose gaps in FDA oversight of imported food
item.description: Most fresh fruits and vegetables imported into the United States come from foreign facilities that federal inspectors have rarely, if ever, visited, a new investigation finds.

item.title: Initial treatment for lower back pain is associated with subsequent risk of opioid use disorder and overdose
item.description: Adults on Medicaid who began treatment for a new bout of low back pain with a higher-dose opioid prescription were about two and a half times as likely to later show signs of opioid use disorder or overdose, according to a study conducted at Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health and NYU Grossman School of Medicine.

item.title: IDSA: Earlier introduction of HPV vaccine improves initiation, completion by age 13
item.description: Introducing the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine at ages 9 to 10 years rather than 11 to 12 years leads to a meaningful difference in initiation and completion of the vaccine series, including initiation and completion by age 13 years, according to a study presented at the annual meeting of the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDWeek), held from Oct. 21 to 24 in Washington, D.C.

item.title: How blocking immune cell signals could make brain tumors easier to remove
item.description: In a new study published in Cancer Cell, researchers at VIB-KU Leuven reduced the spread of glioblastoma by interrupting specific interactions between the brain's immune cells and tumor cells. The discovery points to a possible new therapeutic strategy, in which blocking communication between immune and cancer cells makes tumors more contained and easier to remove.

item.title: Do more cannabis stores near schools mean more teens use cannabis? Our research suggests the answer is complicated
item.description: When Canada legalized recreational cannabis in October 2018, one concern was that more legal stores would make cannabis easier for young people to access and encourage adolescent use. But does having more cannabis retailers near high schools actually mean more students use cannabis?

item.title: Pathology research identifies potential new target for preventing brain metastasis
item.description: Research led by professor of pathology Mikhail Nikiforov, Ph.D., has identified a key mechanism that helps cancer cells spread to the brain, which may lead to a new target for future therapies. The findings were published in the journal Cell Reports in the article "SERINC2-mediated phosphatidylserine remodeling activates protrusion-localized AXL signaling to promote brain metastasis."

item.title: Medicare's prior-authorization pilot test led to an immediate drop in use of services
item.description: For many years, traditional Medicare has operated almost entirely without prior authorization, a requirement that clinicians obtain approval before certain services will be covered. The practice is controversial because it adds paperwork, outside review and other barriers that can delay or deny coverage for recommended treatment. While prior authorization is widely used by commercial insurers and Medicare Advantage, traditional Medicare has historically almost never required it.

item.title: Viruses obey the laws of physics—understanding why they infect people differently could lead to better treatments
item.description: The beauty of physics at the cellular scale is part of what draws biomedical engineers and biologists like us to the field of mechanobiology: the study of how physical forces influence biology.

item.title: Leave home with a plan: What to pack in your medical kit and when to seek care for symptoms abroad
item.description: When people prepare to see a doctor before an international trip, vaccines usually dominate the conversation.
